ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Nonselective alpha blockers: 4

A nonselective alpha antagonist blocks presynaptic feedback as well as vascular alpha1 receptors. Norepinephrine release can rise, contributing to tachycardia. Which receptor effect explains the loss of the normal presynaptic inhibitory feedback?

  1. Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome
  2. Establish alpha blockade before adding beta blockade
  3. Beta2 blockade causing bronchoconstriction
  4. Presynaptic alpha2 blockade
  5. Orthostatic hypotension
Answer and explanation

Presynaptic alpha2 blockade

Blocking alpha2 feedback can increase norepinephrine release and contribute to tachycardia with nonselective alpha antagonists.

Option explanations

Presynaptic alpha2 blockade: Blocking alpha2 feedback can increase norepinephrine release and contribute to tachycardia with nonselective alpha antagonists.

Orthostatic hypotension: Alpha1 blockade reduces the vasoconstrictor response to standing. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome: Alpha1 antagonists, especially tamsulosin, are associated with floppy iris during cataract surgery. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Establish alpha blockade before adding beta blockade: In pheochromocytoma, beta blockade before adequate alpha blockade can worsen vasoconstriction. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Beta2 blockade causing bronchoconstriction: Nonselective beta blockers can aggravate bronchospasm in susceptible patients. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
